The story is remarkably unified, following a clear and logical progression from the discovery of the building's flaw (the beginning), through the prolonged, absurd ordeal of the repairs and the characters' gradual adaptation to it (the middle), to the eventual completion of the work and its lingering psychological aftermath (the end). 

Furthermore, the author weaves recurring motifs and metaphors throughout the narrative to bind the elements together into a harmonious whole. Literary and bureaucratic themes are consistently applied to the physical space (the building is a "typo," the waterproofing is an "envelope," the warped books become "gentle parentheses"). Details introduced early on—such as the dying ficus, the France-shaped stain, the "envelope" metaphor, and the Facilities man's poetic observation that "water has a memory"—are all purposefully recalled in the final paragraphs, bringing the narrative to a deeply satisfying and resonant conclusion about human endurance and adaptation.
